prompt: Two algorithms have comparable fixed per-step costs. One compares all pairs; the other performs linear work over logarithmically many levels. As the input becomes very large, which scaling prediction is justified?

options.text: The linear-times-log algorithm eventually needs less work
options.explanation: Correct. A logarithm grows more slowly than a linear factor, so its total eventually falls below quadratic work.

options.text: Both eventually have the same growth because both use loops
options.explanation: Loop syntax does not determine how many operations execute.

options.text: The pairwise algorithm must always be faster on small inputs
options.explanation: Small-input performance depends on constants; the growth classes do not force that outcome.

options.text: Either growth label predicts exact elapsed time
options.explanation: A count model still needs operation costs and environmental assumptions.

workedExample: Pairwise work gains another proportional factor as input grows. The competing algorithm gains only a logarithmic factor beyond its scan. That difference eventually dominates fixed constants, while finite-size performance still requires measurement.

prompt: You double the length of a large all-distinct input to a pairwise duplicate checker. Assume the same cost per comparison. What should happen to its worst-case work?

options.explanation: The number of candidate pairs grows with input length.
That describes a single scan, not comparing pairs.

options.text: It grows only by one comparison
options.explanation: That resembles adding one logarithmic step, not pair counting.
Correct. There are about twice as many items, each with about twice as many possible partners.

workedExample: The no-duplicate input prevents early exit. Doubling both the number of items and the number of potential partners gives roughly four times the pair count. This predicts counted work; elapsed time may also change if memory or comparison costs change.
